text: Ivan Petrov / Age: 26
Rank/Position: Red Army soldier (private), rifleman
Civilian Occupation: History teacher
Origin: Voronezh city / surrounding area, RSFSR
Ivan Petrov was driven by one thing only: patriotism in its purest form.
His heart beat for the nation and the motherland.
It was almost religious, and he was certain that this devotion,
this worship of home, was what kept him alive.
Doctors told his parents early on that he was a sick, fragile boy,
not built for this world.
<i>“Protect him from everything, even from the wind.
There's no medicine I can prescribe for what he has,”
the doctor explained to his parents, who took the advice to heart.
They kept him wrapped in comfort.
The boy begged in vain for the same treatment
his siblings and other children his age got.
They wouldn't even let him work summers to earn a little money.
They wouldn't let him play outside in daylight either —
he was allowed out only at dusk, when the sun couldn't burn him,
and even then only as far from the house
as his mother could watch through the kitchen window.
The other children made it even worse, pushing him out for his weak build.
They didn't like playing with him, because whichever team he was put on,
whether they were playing football or war,
it was guaranteed he'd be a handicap to his teammates.
Maybe that's why it's no surprise that after a while he stopped asking
to go outside with the others.
He stayed in his room instead. He liked the half-dark the lowered blinds created,
and with his thick-framed glasses — which he was ashamed to wear in front of other boys —
perched on his nose, squinting hard, he devoured
volume after volume from his father's inexhaustible library.
It didn't take long for him to convince himself
that it was better to read about the injustices done to his homeland
during the Napoleonic wars than to choke in the dust outside,
and that Lenin's immortal ideas could soothe an ordinary Russian youth
even when his chest began to sting like an old man's.
Ivan formed a belief as solid as iron: that Russia had been robbed of its greatness again and again,
or at least, the West had tried to rob it, and it didn't matter
which conquerors came to defile the holy soil —
in the end, they always failed.
That belief is why he became a history teacher.
So he could pass the idea of national greatness
into as many unpolished minds as possible,
in his modest way helping to ensure
that the motherland stays in good hands in the generations to come.
But daytime speeches in a classroom didn't fully satisfy his hunger for justice,
so in the evenings he went to pubs and cafés
and, like a drunk —
though he never drank a drop of alcohol —
with a flushed face and shining eyes he preached, climbing onto chairs and
tables, sometimes straight onto the counter, about what should be done
to the nations that threaten Mother Russia.
So when the motherland needed him most, there was never any question
of whether he would go to war.
He knew there were cowardly traitors who would fold their hands in gratitude
if their poor health excused them from service,
but Ivan was of course not one of them.
No, on the contrary: he reached into his pocket and used a significant portion
of the money he'd inherited from his parents to grease the right palms,
to persuade the decision-making doctors to look away from his irregular heartbeat
and the lungs that worked at only seventy percent capacity.
So now Ivan leans out of the trench and fires, keeps firing,
and sings The Sacred War at the top of his lungs.
He's the most surprised of all that his voice doesn't crack,
that his breathing doesn't whistle.
The sound comes out clean and clear into the frozen air,
as if the cold couldn't touch him,
as if the bullets of men who fight without conviction couldn't either.
And if death does catch him here, Ivan isn't afraid.
He only hopes the sun will come out,
that the thick crust of ice over the ground will finally soften,
so the sweet motherland, his mother earth, can drink to the last drop the blood of her fragile child.
